analysis: The closest composition integrates climate science, environmental processes and biodiversity with geospatial analysis, field and laboratory methods for soils and aquifers, and quantitative inference. Marine Biology adds production and habitat processes, fisheries and coastal pressures, with Introduction to Biodiversity placed earlier. The governance composition retains the environmental and quantitative foundation and replaces advanced sustainability research with a theory-guided empirical civil-society investigation, after prior environmental-justice and methods coursework. It combines formal institutions, international law, conflict, EU policy, environmental justice and public climate communication. The business composition builds from economics and entrepreneurship to market research, innovation and corporate governance. Market Research applies empirical inquiry to business decisions, while renewable energy, life-cycle analysis and experimental materials recovery provide distinct sustainability substance. The three routes retain generator ownership. The closest handles sustainable food through sustainable farming and the linked environmental systems; the business option handles the energy side through renewable design and resources. The three replacements support the existing directions, while none is described as replicating the unavailable partner research project. The alignment distinguishes applied UCR coursework from a dedicated Utrecht ecology field course, consultancy and compulsory thesis.

alignment.rationale: Both use interdisciplinary concepts to examine sustainability challenges. UCR introduces planetary boundaries and scientific tools through modelling and laboratory work.
Both study interactions among natural processes. UCR focuses on Earth systems, geology and field evidence.
Both examine climate processes, impacts and possible responses. Utrecht deepens the topic within the track.
Both examine biodiversity and ecological processes. Utrecht specialises in landscape ecology and conservation at advanced level.
Both examine water in soils and related natural systems. UCR focuses on soils and shallow aquifers, while Utrecht integrates water and ecosystem processes.
Utrecht surveys social-science approaches to sustainability. UCR develops related perspectives across economics, governance and environmental justice courses.
Both examine sustainability transitions, actors and possible interventions. Utrecht brings the perspectives together in a project. UCR focuses on governance and policy evaluation.
Both use chemistry to investigate environmental problems. UCR focuses on recovering materials and assessing remediation processes.
Both examine chemical processes and contaminants in environmental systems. Utrecht gives additional attention to human exposure and health.
Both develop mathematical tools for analysing systems. Utrecht embeds the tools in its sustainability programme.
Both develop research design and evidence skills. UCR adds statistical inference and quantitative analysis within this course.
Both develop statistical inference and hypothesis testing. UCR gives greater emphasis to mathematical foundations and simulation.
Both integrate evidence and disciplinary perspectives in an applied sustainability project. Utrecht uses fieldwork and stakeholder research on Texel. UCR investigates sustainability campaigns.
Utrecht requires a dedicated ecological field research course. UCR develops related field and laboratory skills in courses including Soils & Aquifers.
Utrecht offers philosophy of science and ethics as an intermediate major choice.
Utrecht requires a 15 EC individual thesis. UCR’s 15 EC optional independent research is shown separately from the scheduled courses.
Utrecht requires a separate consultancy project addressing an external organisation’s question.
Choose 45 EC, with at least 15 EC at intermediate or advanced level. Options include extra major courses, a minor, study abroad or an internship. External courses require approval.
